UP Weather Today: लखनऊ में बढ़ेगा तापमान, पूर्वी यूपी में झमाझम बरसेंगे बादल; IMD ने किया अलर्ट
UP Weather Update Today: लखनऊ में शनिवार को बारिश थमने के बाद उमस बढ़ी, जबकि रविवार को तापमान में आंशिक वृद्धि की संभावना है। मौसम विभाग ने पूर्वी उत्तर प्रदेश में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट जारी किया है, वहीं लखनऊ में हल्की बौछारें पड़ सकती हैं।
HighLights
लखनऊ में शनिवार को बारिश थमने से बढ़ी उमस।
रविवार को लखनऊ का तापमान बढ़ने की संभावना है।
पूर्वी उत्तर प्रदेश में भारी बारिश का अलर्ट जारी।
जागरण संवाददाता, लखनऊ। पिछले दो दिनों से लखनऊ (Lucknow Rain Update) में हो रही झमाझम बारिश का सिलसिला शनिवार को कुछ थम गया। शनिवार सुबह लखनऊ और आसपास के जिलों में बादल छाए रहे। इससे सुबह हल्की बारिश ने मौसम खुशनुमा बना दिया।
हालांकि दोपहर बाद उमस से लोगों को परेशान भी किया। रविवार को लखनऊ के न्यूतनम और अधिकतम तापमान में आंशिक वृद्धि होगी। हालांकि पूर्वी उत्तर प्रदेश में झमाझम बारिश की संभावना है।
शनिवार को लखनऊ का अधिकतम तापमान 32.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, जो कि सामान्य से एक डिग्री सेल्सियस कम रहा। इसी तरह न्यूनतम तापमान 25.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, यह सामान्य से 0.4 डिग्री अधिक था।

मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक रविवार को लखनऊ और आसपास बादल छाए रहेंगे। कहीं -कहीं हल्की बौछार भी हो सकती है। अधिकतम तापमान 33 और न्यूनतम 27 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रह सकता है। पूर्वी उत्तर प्रदेश में भारी बारिश के आसार हैँ।

articles.full_text:
Bihar Weather Update: बिहार के कई इलाकों में बारिश के आसार, तापमान बढ़ने से उमस बढ़ाएगी परेशानी
बिहार में मानसून की सक्रियता कम होने से भारी वर्षा में कमी आई है, जिससे तापमान में वृद्धि और उमस बनी हुई है। पटना सहित 19 जिलों में तापमान बढ़ा है, हालांकि कुछ स्थानों पर छिटपुट वर्षा की संभावना है।
HighLights
बिहार में मानसून की सक्रियता में कमी आई है।
पटना सहित 19 जिलों के तापमान में वृद्धि दर्ज।
अगले 24 घंटे में छिटपुट वर्षा के आसार।
जागरण संवाददाता, पटना। Bihar Weather Update: बिहार में मानसून की सक्रियता कम होने के साथ भारी वर्षा में कमी आई है। इसके कारण तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव की स्थिति बने होने के साथ उमस का प्रभाव बना रहेगा। शनिवार को पटना सहित 19 जिलों के अधिकतम तापमान में वृद्धि दर्ज की गई।
पटना का अधिकतम तापमान 37.0 डिग्री सेल्सियस एवं 37.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस के साथ अररिया के फारबिसगंज में सर्वाधिक तापमान दर्ज किया गया। बीते 24 घंटे के दौरान प्रदेश के अलग-अलग भागों में वर्षा दर्ज की गई। समस्तीपुर के कल्याणपुर में 52.4 मिमी सर्वाधिक वर्षा दर्ज की गई।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, मानसून ट्रफ अमृतसर, हरदोई और मध्यप्रदेश के आसपास इलाकों से जमशेदपुर, दीघा होते हुए बंगाल की खाड़ी से होकर गुजर रही है। इनके प्रभाव से अलग-अलग भागों में छिटपुट वर्षा की संभावना है।
छुटपुट बारिश के आसार
मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र पटना के अनुसार अगले 24 घंटे के दौरान राजधानी सहित प्रदेश के ज्यादातर भागों में बादलों की आवाजाही बने होने के साथ कई स्थानों पर छिटपुट वर्षा के आसार हैं।
उत्तर व दक्षिण भागों के कुछ स्थानों पर 30-40 किमी प्रतिघंटा की रफ्तार से हवा चलने के आसार हैं। प्रदेश के अलग-अलग भागों में मेघ गर्जन, वज्रपात को लेकर चेतावनी जारी की गई है। तीन से चार दिनों के दौरान तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव की स्थिति बने रहने की संभावना है।
शनिवार को पटना सहित आसपास इलाकों में बादलों की आवाजाही बने होने के साथ तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव के साथ उमस का प्रभाव बना रहा। कुछ स्थानों पर हल्की बूंदाबांदी की स्थिति बनी रही।
इन स्थानों पर दर्ज हुई वर्षा
पश्चिम चंपारण के चनपटिया में 20.4 मिमी, गोपालंज के मांझा में 16.8 मिमी, बांका के बौसी में 16.6 मिमी, पूर्णिया के कीर्तियानंद नगर में 14.0 मिमी, गोपालगंज के कोचायकोट में 8.2 मिमी, वैशाली के भगवानपुर में 8.2 मिमी, शेखपुरा के घाट कुसुंबा में 7.6 मिमी, भागलपुर के पीरपाती में 6.6 मिमी, नवादा के अकबरपुर में 6.6 मिमी, औरंगाबाद के बारूण में 6.4 मिमी, सिवान में 5.4 मिमी, गोपालगंज के भोरे में 5.2 मिमी, रोहतास के नौहट्टा में 4.6 मिमी, बक्सर के राजपुर में 4.6 मिमी, भागलपुर के बीहपुर में 3.8 मिमी, गोपालगंज में 3.2 मिमी, समस्तीपुर के वारिसनगर में 2.6 मिमी, जमुई में 2.4 मिमी, बांका के चंदन में 2.4 मिमी, भागलपुर के खरीक में 2.4 मिमी वर्षा दर्ज की गई।

articles.full_text:
How to avoid breaking down in extreme weather
Drivers should be prepared for forecast thundery showers following the recent heatwave, a motoring organisation has said.
The Hampshire-based AA said it saw an increase in roadside recoveries due to extreme heat, with flat batteries, cooling system breakdowns and tyre trouble among recent issues.
The Basingstoke-based company said hard ground could mean considerable surface run-off during sudden heavy rain in coming weeks.
On patrol in the Windsor and Maidenhead area of Berkshire, the AA's Lee Morley said: "Conditions can change incredibly quickly when a thundery downpour hits.
"After such a long spell of hot and dry weather, drivers may not be expecting roads to suddenly become covered in surface water or even flooded, so they need to be ready to adapt quickly," he added.
"Slow down, increase the distance between you and the vehicle ahead and avoid sudden braking or sharp steering."
He told people to never risk driving through floodwater, which could gather quickly because of the hard ground.
"If water looks too deep or is moving, turn around and find another route," Morley added.
"You cannot always tell how deep it is from behind the wheel, and there could be damage or other hazards hidden underneath. A short delay or diversion is always preferable to putting yourself, your passengers or your vehicle at risk."
Analysis from the AA found that one in 10 breakdowns in hot weather were potentially avoidable, while more than a third of its calls were linked to driver awareness issues like flat batteries, using the wrong fuel or charging issues in electric vehicles.
Holiday traffic can also play its part causing additional heat in the clutch and transmission components.
Morley said drivers can prepare themselves.
"Travelling at this time of year with the heat we advise carrying at least a litre of water per person in the vehicle," he said.
"Checking the engine oil, coolant levels, tyre pressures - little bits and pieces like that can help prevent a breakdown."

Rain, thunderstorms and extreme heat forecast in Kazakhstan Aug 23
Heavy rainfall is expected in the northwest, north, central regions and mountainous areas of the southeast.
Dry conditions will prevail in the west, southwest and east. Strong winds are forecast nationwide, with dust storms in the south and foggy conditions in the northern, eastern and central areas.
Daytime temperatures will rise sharply, with +35°C in West Kazakhstan region, +35+38°C in Atyrau region, and +38+42°C in Mangystau region.
Authorities warn of high fire danger in Kostanay region, south of Akmola region, northwest of West Kazakhstan and East Kazakhstan regions, center of Aktobe region, east of Zhambyl, Pavlodar, Almaty regions, as well as west of Abai region.
An extreme fire hazard is forecast in Kyzylorda, Turkistan, Zhambyl, Atyrau, West Kazakhstan, Aktobe, Almaty, Zhetysu, Ulytau regions, in the south and southeast of Kostanay region, west and north of Mangystau region, west, south, east and center of Karaganda region, west of Akmola region, south of East Kazakhstan region and Abai region.

articles.title: Rainwater stored on rooftops could help cities beat extreme heat - Earth.com
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Rainwater stored on rooftops could help cities beat extreme heat
A Tokyo model suggests stored rainwater could cool hot roofs, reduce air conditioning demand, and ease some extreme heat.
Spray water on a hot roof and the building underneath stays cooler. In hot climates, cities keep passing on that idea because sprinklers on every rooftop would use water a city can’t spare in a heatwave.
Rain that already fell on those roofs is the exception, and a new model of one Tokyo neighborhood estimates that catching it can cut the energy air conditioning uses.
How much it saves depends on the timing more than the hardware. A bigger tank matters less than the temperature that starts the spray.
Zhonghua Zheng, an associate professor in the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Manchester (UoM), built the system with PhD researcher Junjie Yu and four co-authors.
They wrote the tank and the sprinklers into the Community Land Model Urban, a simulation of how a city’s roofs, walls, and streets trade heat and water with the air. The NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research built that model; the Manchester team added the plumbing.
In an interview with Earth.com, Zheng was asked which finding he most wanted to highlight.
“One important finding is that the temperature at which sprinkling begins matters more than either tank size or sprinkling intensity,” he said.
The roof’s own heat starts the spray
Watering a roof works. A 2025 study found that spraying can lower a roof’s surface temperature by 10°F to 35°F (5.5°C to 19.5°C). The constraint has always been the water.
Rain landing on a roof normally evaporates, puddles or runs off down the drain. In this design, the runoff goes into a tank instead and waits there until the roof gets hot enough to need it.
The sprinklers switch on when the roof surface passes a set temperature, and the team let that threshold range from 95°F to 149°F (35°C to 65°C). Roofs get much hotter than the street air, so the number refers to the roof itself.
Yu and Zheng sampled 400 combinations of tank size, spray rate, and trigger temperature, then ran each through the model. A higher trigger generally meant more air conditioning energy. With the trigger set low, the spray rate began to matter too.
Roof runoff is too dirty for drinking or washing, so the tank feeds only the sprinklers, and only from June through September. In the best runs, the water came on around 9 a.m. and stopped around 7 p.m.
Bigger tanks stopped paying off
The neighborhood in the model is a 0.23-square-mile patch of Yoyogi, Tokyo, roughly 110 football fields, with 1,996 roofs and buildings averaging 30 feet (9 m) tall.
Tank size here is expressed as the depth of water that would cover the roof when the tank is full. The smallest tank holds about 0.17 inch (4.37 mm) and the biggest holds 0.79 inch (19.99 mm).
The team’s search had two goals, less air conditioning energy and the smallest tank that could deliver it. It ran on a machine-learning copy of the climate model, because the full version is too slow.
Among the best combinations, the neighborhood with the smallest tank used 1,600.76 megawatt-hours of air conditioning a year. Moving to the 0.17-inch tank saved about 49 megawatt-hours. Saving the next 49 took storage 4.6 times larger.
So the first half of the saving comes at little cost, and the rest costs almost five times the tank. Water behaves the same way.
“Once the roof was sufficiently wet, adding more water produced diminishing cooling and energy-saving benefits,” Zheng told Earth.com.
A roof cools as the water on it evaporates. Once the surface is soaked, extra spray just lies there, and in the model a long, gentle soak beat a short, heavy one.
Extreme heat hours fell across the block
The street cools for two reasons. Wet roofs evaporate water, and buildings running less air conditioning push less waste heat into the urban heat island around them.
Over ten simulated summers, the sprinklers cut the time roofs spent at unusually high temperatures by roughly 590 to 1,220 hours. Those were temperatures the roofs reached only 5% of the time without the system.
Street-level air cooled less, but it still cooled: hours above 95°F (35°C) fell by 86 to 298 across the decade, or about 9 to 30 hours a summer.
Comfort improved least. Water sprayed on a roof adds moisture to the air, and humidity is part of what makes heat dangerous.
The humidex combines temperature and humidity into a single reading of heat stress. The block spent only 3.5 to 19.5 fewer hours above 46, the level the authors treat as great discomfort. With the largest tanks, those hours started to climb again.
Tanks also caught water that would have poured off the roofs. Extreme runoff eased steadily as storage grew, by five hours at the small end and 51 at the large one.
Heatwaves arrived less often
A heatwave here is three days in a row at or above 95°F (35°C). The team counted them twice, once breaking the run whenever a cooler day interrupted it, and once allowing one cooler day inside.
In the simulations, the block had fewer heatwave days under both counts. The biggest tanks cut the most, and the events arrived less often and peaked slightly cooler.
Average length didn’t follow. Under the stricter count it edged up, because the sprinklers were ending short heatwaves and leaving the long ones to make up more of what remained. Under the looser count it fell.
Warmer years produced bigger savings
The ten summers weren’t equally hot, and the hotter ones saved more energy. That pattern was weak in runs with small tanks and moderately strong with the biggest ones. Yearly rainfall tracked the savings less closely than temperature did.
Zheng said the optimized system lowered air conditioning demand, extreme roof and air temperatures, heatwave days, and extreme runoff. The bigger savings in hotter years, he said, suggest the benefits could become more valuable as the climate warms.
The World Health Organization estimates that about 125 million more people were exposed to extreme heatwaves in 2016 than in 2000.
Asked by Earth.com whether it would work in a drier city than Tokyo, Zheng said it might, with changes to suit local conditions.
“Limited rainfall could make it less effective or require another water source,” he said.
A pilot has to come first
Nothing here was measured on a real roof. The city model behind it has been checked against a tower of instruments in Yoyogi, and it tracks the measured radiation closely and the heat and moisture flows less well. But the tank and the sprinklers don’t exist outside the code.
One quirk of the model rides with the findings. Air just above the roofs mixes freely with air in the streets below, so where that link is weaker, the street-level cooling would come out smaller.
Mold grows on a roof that stays wet, sprinkling wears at roofing material, rules on collecting rainwater differ from city to city, and tanks and their upkeep cost money. Reflective cool roofs – another way to cool the same buildings – use no water at all.
Zheng said costs, regulations and moisture risks all need assessing. Then comes the part no simulation can do.
“A city would need pilot testing, suitable roofs and drainage, sufficient local rainfall, and systems for monitoring and maintenance,” Zheng said.
Only a real tank on a real roof, through one Tokyo August, can turn these estimates into measurements.
The full study was published in the journal Earth’s Future.

Despite a rain forecast for the second consecutive day, Rajasthan received very little rainfall. The Meteorological Department had issued a yellow alert for 18 districts on Saturday, but only four districts recorded light rain.
The weather remained clear across the rest of the state. The department has now issued a yellow alert for 14 districts on Sunday. With the monsoon remaining sluggish, daytime temperatures have risen, increasing heat and humidity.
Major monsoon updates
Dholpur records highest rainfall
Dholpur's Rajakhera recorded the highest rainfall on Saturday at 21mm. Basedi received 4mm, Laxmangarh in Alwar 10mm, Kathumar 5mm and Nagar in Bharatpur 3mm. Light drizzle was also reported in Chikli, Dungarpur.
The weather remained completely clear across Jaipur, Ajmer, Bikaner, Jodhpur, Kota and Udaipur divisions. With no rain in Chittorgarh, Kota, Pilani, Sikar, Churu and Ganganagar, temperatures rose to as much as 3°C above normal.
Temperatures reach 35°C or higher in nine cities
The lack of rain has allowed heat and humidity to persist across the state. On Saturday, nine cities recorded maximum temperatures of 35°C or above. Ganganagar recorded the state's highest maximum temperature at 39.6°C.
Monsoon trough remains stalled in the north
Weather experts said the monsoon trough has remained north of its normal position for the past few days.
It is currently passing through Amritsar, Najibabad and Hardoi, then through a well-marked low-pressure area over eastern Madhya Pradesh, before extending via Jamshedpur and Digha to the Bay of Bengal.
As a result, several areas of Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, eastern Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand are receiving good rainfall.
Weather conditions in major Rajasthan districts
Jaipur
The weak spell of rain has pushed temperatures up in Jaipur. The maximum temperature reached 35°C, which was 2.2°C above normal, while the minimum was 26.6°C. Light sunshine continued through the day. Some areas saw light clouds in the evening, but there was no rain.
Udaipur
The sky remained overcast from Saturday morning, although the sun appeared during the day. After 4pm, dense clouds covered the city and a cool breeze began to blow. There was no rain anywhere in Udaipur city or across the district. The maximum temperature was 32.1°C and the minimum was 22.6°C.
Alwar
Strong sunshine kept Alwar hot throughout the day, with the maximum temperature reaching around 37°C. Clouds suddenly covered the district in the evening. According to the Meteorological Department, Alwar could receive light rain accompanied by thunder and lightning until August 27.
Kota
The spell of rain has weakened in Kota. Despite Saturday's alert, the district received no rain, while heat and humidity troubled residents. The maximum temperature was 34.3°C and the minimum was 25.8°C. The Meteorological Department has issued a yellow rain alert for the Kota division until August 24.
Ajmer
The sluggish monsoon continued in Ajmer on Saturday. Despite the rain forecast, sunshine and heat persisted throughout the day. The maximum temperature was 32.9°C, while the minimum was 23.3°C.
Jodhpur
Jodhpur experienced generally normal weather on Saturday. Sunshine during the day increased humidity. The maximum temperature was 33.6°C, which was 0.4°C below normal, while the minimum temperature was 26.4°C.
The Meteorological Department has forecast no rain in Jodhpur for the next five days.
Sikar
Light clouds covered Sikar on Saturday morning before bright sunshine appeared. Clouds gathered again after 3pm, followed by a light breeze in the evening. No rain was recorded anywhere in the district. According to the Meteorological Centre, the maximum temperature was 35.5°C and the minimum was 24.9°C.

articles.full_text:
THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned that widespread rain is likely in the state on Sunday. The warning is in the backdrop of the formation of a cyclonic circulation in the Bay of Bengal and over the coasts of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. In this situation, yellow alert has been issued in Kannur, Kozhikode and Wayanad today. The rain is intensifying in the state after a short gap. Fishing is banned on the coasts of Kerala and Lakshadweep.
Fishermen and coastal residents have been cautioned as there is a possibility of a rough sea. As the sea is likely to intensify, they should move away from the danger areas as per the instructions of the authorities. Launching small boats and yachts into the sea should be avoided during this time. Bringing fishing vessels back to shore is just as dangerous as launching them into the sea during periods when there is a possibility of the Kallakkadal phenomenon and high waves. So, the IMD has stated that it is necessary to avoid launching oats into the sea and bringing them ashore when the waves are intensifying.
